**From the Mithridatic Wars, First Century BC**

Our general was elsewhere, but we drowned.
While he rested, he sent us homeward
with the bulk of his spoils
that had weighed his army down.

The thrashing storm that caught us
cracked open the hulls
and made us offerings to the seafloor—
a rain of statues, gold, and men.

Released from service, done with war,
the crash and hiss now muted,
we fell through streams of creatures
whose lives held true purpose.

We settled amid treasure looted
from the temples of rubbled Athenian Greece;
among us, bronze and marble gods and goddesses
moored without grace,
passed over by incurious fish.

Their power was never meant to buoy us—
our pleasures were but incidental gifts—
yet, stirred by their radiance in our dust,
we had lent them our voices.

Their faces, wings, and limbs
lie here now with our sanded bones
and our stilled instruments.

Little crabs attempt to don rings
set with agate and amethyst,
and many an octopus,
seeking an hour's rest,
finds shelter in our brain-cases.

So we remain of use.

---

I preserved every image, event, and idea from your original—the general's absence, the storm, the sunken treasure, the fish, the crabs and octopus—while smoothing the cadence, sharpening transitions, and elevating word choice for a more polished, literary tone. Let me know if you'd like the language pushed even further toward formality, or kept closer to the starker, more elemental voice of the original.

**From the Mithridatic Wars, 1st century BC**

Our commander stood far off when the waters claimed us.
While he took his ease, he sent us toward home,
burdened with the plunder
that had slowed his marching legions.
A violent squall
seized our vessels and split them open,
scattering our cargo to the depths below —
a downpour of carved figures, precious metal, and human forms.
Freed at last from duty,
our warring days behind us,
the tumult and roar now silenced,
we sank past schools of living things
pursuing their own small purposes.
We came to rest alongside treasures stripped
from the shattered temples of ancient Athens;
bronze and marble deities drifted beside us,
anchored without dignity,
ignored by fish who paid us no mind.
Never meant to keep us afloat,
their divine strength offered us only accidental comfort —
yet dazzled by their glow within our murk,
we had once lent them our worship.
Now their broken features, wings, and limbs
rest among our weathered remains
and our silent equipment.
Small crabs try to slip into
rings studded with agate and amethyst,
while octopuses, searching for
a moment's peace,
tuck themselves into the hollows of our skulls.
And so, even now, we serve some purpose still.
outputs.L3:
# The Silent Fall

A general once made a fateful decision that would echo through history: he ordered his soldiers home by sea, their ships laden with the spoils of conquest, while he himself remained behind on foreign soil. Perhaps he sought to oversee some final matter of state, or perhaps fate simply spared him from what was to come. For as the fleet set sail, heavy with plunder and dreams of homecoming, the sky darkened with a violence that no soldier could have anticipated. A storm of merciless fury descended upon the waters, and in its wake, it left nothing but devastation—ships splintered like kindling, men swallowed by the churning sea, and the treasures they carried scattered across the ocean floor like forgotten offerings to some indifferent god.

The soldiers, who had survived the horrors of war only to be freed at last from military service, found no triumphant return awaiting them. Instead, they sank silently through the darkening depths, descending past schools of fish and creatures of the deep who continued their ancient rhythms, indifferent to the human tragedy unfolding around them. The sea claimed these men not as conquerors but as strangers, their bodies drifting downward to settle among a world that had never known war, glory, or plunder.

As the wreckage came to rest upon the ocean floor, it did so alongside the very treasures the soldiers had carried—sacred objects looted from the temples of Athens, now separated from their divine purpose. Bronze and marble figures of gods and goddesses, once revered in gleaming sanctuaries and honored with prayer and sacrifice, now lay scattered and undignified upon the silt, surrounded by fish who swam past without comprehension, oblivious to the majesty these figures once commanded.

And yet, though these divine statues possessed no true power to calm the storm or spare a single life, the sailors who had carried them across the sea had not seen them as mere cargo. In their final moments, and throughout the long voyage before the tempest struck, the men had regarded these figures with something like reverence—not because they believed the stone and bronze could truly save them, but because even in the depths of disaster, beauty commanded its own kind of worship. The statues, silent and lifeless as they were, had been given voice by human awe, spoken to and honored simply because their crafted forms stirred something sacred in those who beheld them.

Now, centuries removed from that fateful storm, the remains of both mortal men and immortal gods have found an unexpected second purpose beneath the waves. What was once tragedy has become sanctuary: crabs scuttle among the ruins, adorning themselves with fragments of bronze and marble as though continuing some unconscious tribute to beauty. Octopuses, seeking shelter from the dangers of the open sea, make their homes within the hollow skulls of the drowned soldiers, finding refuge in the very remains that once housed thought, fear, and hope. In this quiet transformation, the ocean has woven together the fates of men and gods alike, granting them both a strange and humbling afterlife—not as symbols of empire or divinity, but as shelter for the small and living creatures who now call the deep their home.
outputs.L4:
**The Sunken Gods**

In the years when Mithridates set the East ablaze,
when Rome's legions marched through burning Pontic days,
the soldiers loaded galleys deep with Grecian spoil—
bronze Apollos, marble Venus, torn from sacred soil.

They sailed for home with laughter, with the clink of stolen gold,
with statues of the deathless ones packed tight into the hold,
believing that the gods they'd stripped from temple and from shrine
would guard them now as cargo, would prove their fates benign.

But the sea does not remember conquest, does not care for creed—
a storm rose up at midnight with a dark and ancient need.
The waves broke over gunwales, the masts cracked like old bone,
and soldiers who had plundered heaven sank to depths unknown.

They called upon the marble gods still lashed within the hold,
they screamed the names of Zeus and Ares as the waters rolled,
but bronze does not hear pleading, and stone does not know grief—
the gods went down in silence, offering no relief.

So soldier and so statue sank together through the dark,
past all the light of living, past the last and dying spark,
and settled on the sea floor in a strange and common grave—
the conqueror and conquered, the plunderer and the brave.

Now centuries have drifted like the silt that buries bone,
and what was templed marble has become a coral throne.
The crabs have made their houses in the folds of Athena's gown,
the octopus now nestles where the warrior's blade went down.

There is no glory here, no monument to war,
no epitaph in Latin on this cold and sunken floor—
only tentacles curling round a god's unseeing eye,
only claws that scuttle where the drowned once learned to die.

And is it not a mercy, this quiet, creeping tide,
that gives the toppled idols something more than empty pride?
That gives the bones of soldiers, who once served with sword in hand,
a purpose in the deep sea they could not find on land?

The gods could not save sailors, and the sailors could not save
the treasures that they'd stolen from a conquered people's grave.
But now in mutual ruin, in this cold and briny bed,
new life has found a shelter in the kingdom of the dead.

So let the marble crumble, let the bronze grow green with age—
the sea has written over war's unfinished, bloody page.
No hero rests in honor, no god stands proud and tall,
but crab and octopus have made a peace that outlasts all.
outputs.L5:
# The Mithridatic Wars: Rome's Struggle for the East

From the late second century BCE through the early first century BCE, the Roman Republic found itself engaged in a series of brutal conflicts with the Kingdom of Pontus, a powerful state located in Asia Minor along the shores of the Black Sea. These conflicts, known collectively as the Mithridatic Wars, were named after their central antagonist: King Mithridates VI Eupator, one of the most formidable enemies Rome ever faced.

Mithridates VI ascended to the Pontic throne as a young man and quickly began expanding his kingdom's influence throughout Anatolia and the Black Sea region. His ambitions inevitably brought him into conflict with Roman interests in the East, setting the stage for three major wars fought between 89 BCE and 63 BCE.

**The First Mithridatic War (89–85 BCE)**

The initial conflict erupted when Mithridates invaded the Roman province of Asia, exploiting local resentment against Roman tax collectors and administrators. In a shocking display of his power, Mithridates orchestrated the infamous "Asiatic Vespers," a coordinated massacre in which tens of thousands of Roman and Italian citizens living in Asia Minor were killed in a single day. Rome responded by dispatching Lucius Cornelius Sulla, who eventually forced Mithridates to accept peace terms after reclaiming Greek territories the Pontic king had seized.

**The Second Mithridatic War (83–81 BCE)**

A shorter and less decisive conflict followed, triggered by Roman commander Lucius Licinius Murena's provocative actions in Pontic territory. This war ended without significant changes to the territorial status quo.

**The Third Mithridatic War (73–63 BCE)**

The final and most extensive phase of the conflict saw Mithridates renew hostilities, this time facing Roman generals Lucullus and later Pompey the Great. Despite years of fierce resistance and notable early victories, Mithridates was ultimately defeated. Cornered and betrayed even by his own son, the aging king chose suicide rather than capture in 63 BCE, bringing an end to decades of warfare.

**Legacy**

From these prolonged conflicts, Rome emerged with significantly expanded control over Asia Minor and the broader eastern Mediterranean. The wars demonstrated both the resilience of Mithridates as a strategic adversary and the ultimate military supremacy of Rome, paving the way for further Roman expansion into the Near East in the decades that followed.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a historical poem from the perspective of drowned Roman soldiers whose ship carrying looted Greek statues sank during the Mithridatic Wars.
counterfactuals.output:
# Cargo of Marble

We went down with the gods we stole,
their marble eyes still wide with peace
while ours went wide with water.
Sulla's orders, Sulla's gold—
we were only meant to carry,
not to keep.

The Athena did not weep for us.
Why should she? We took her from her hill,
wrapped her in canvas like a corpse
already, roped her to the deck
beside the Apollo with his lyre
that never learned to swim.

The storm came up from Aegean dark
the way old wrongs do—
sudden, righteous, unconcerned
with the difference between
a soldier and a sack of plunder.
We were cargo too, in the end.

I remember Titus screaming for the gods
we'd bagged like grain below,
as if Poseidon might forgive a fleet
that carried his own kin as booty,
chained in bronze and stone,
their sea now closing over ships and thieves alike.

We sink together now, the marble and the men,
two thousand years of settling
into silt and sediment and story.
Somewhere above, Rome forgot us—
another lost supply, another cost
of empire's appetite.

But down here in the blue-black quiet
where the statues finally stand
where they were always meant to be—
in water, in Greece, unmoved—
we soldiers lie beside the gods we robbed,
guarding what we could not keep,

drowned custodians of theft,
our breastplates rusting into reef,
Athena's stone face inches from my own,
both of us witnesses now
to how the sea keeps
what the land let go.

We are the empire's small mistake,
a shipment lost, a line in someone's ledger—
but here, we are the only ones who stayed
with what we stole. Perhaps
that is its own slow penance:
to lie forever with the beautiful, the taken,

to become, ourselves,
the treasure that the water hides.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a free verse poem imagining the sunken wreck of a Roman ship full of plundered Athenian art, told from the viewpoint of the dead sailors.
counterfactuals.output:
**Cargo**

We went down with the gods in our hold,
Athena's own marble eyes still wide
in the dark, painted lids that never learned
to close against seawater.

Three hundred years we have lain here
becoming reef, becoming rust-flower,
becoming the coral's excuse for existing,
and still the bronze youths stand at attention
in the ribs of the ship, waiting
for a triumph that will not come.

We were only sailors. We did not choose
what filled the hold—the friezes torn
from temples that watched the Persians burn once
and thought that was the worst of it,
the philosopher's face in stone, mouth
still open mid-argument, the small
gold owls meant for some senator's mantle,
proof of Rome's improving taste.

Someone above us, once,
called this glory. Called it *spoils*,
as if the word made clean
what hands had pried from pediments
with the patience of men who believe
beauty is a debt owed to the strong.

Now the octopus makes her home
in the empty socket where a spear-arm
used to be. Now the small fish
school through the ribs of dancing girls
who have not danced in centuries
and do not seem to mind the stillness—
they were stone all along, we understand that now,
the way you understand a thing only
by becoming its neighbor in the deep.

We drowned reaching for what wasn't ours.
The weight that sank us was the weight
of someone else's history, wrapped
in oiled cloth and rope, stowed careful
as a secret. We went under
still gripping lines that led nowhere,
still calling out in Latin
to a shore that had already
stopped listening.

Down here the marble does not care
whose empire claimed it.
It has outlasted us the way stone
outlasts every claim made on it—
not by strength, but by simply
continuing to be itself
long after the hands
that carried it away
have softened into sand,
have become
another kind of silence
at the bottom of the sea,
another kind of art
no living eye will ever
call plunder,
or masterpiece,
or ours.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poem about an ancient shipwreck where soldiers and stolen statues of gods now share the seabed, blending myth, war, and the ocean's slow reclamation.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Sunken Fleet

Below the reach of anchor and of light,
where pressure folds the years like paper thin,
the galley sleeps within its stony night,
its ribs grown soft with barnacle and fin.

The bronze gods lie where they were bound to sail—
stolen from temples, wrapped in oiled cloth,
plunder promised for a conqueror's tale,
now tangled in the sea's slow, patient wrath.

Poseidon's stolen brother, cast in bronze,
still grips a trident rusted at the tine,
beside him lies a soldier's skull that dons
a crown of coral where his helm's design

once caught the sun on decks now dark as pitch.
They fought for gold, for glory, or for God,
and here they rest—no difference, no stitch
of rank between the marble and the sod

they've both become. The captain's bones recline
against a goddess missing half her face,
as if in death they'd forged some final line
of truce that war denied them in their place.

The current moves like breath through empty holds,
where amphorae still hum with vanished wine,
and slowly, slowly, the deep unfolds
its patient work—dissolving the design

of empire, plunder, conquest, holy claim.
The gods who once demanded blood and gold
now feed the anemone, all the same
as those who died to keep them bought and sold.

No hymn is sung here but the whale's low song,
no war is fought but tide against the stone.
The sea does not remember right or wrong—
it only knows to make the lost its own.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical, first-person plural poem set after a naval disaster in antiquity, describing how the sunken treasure and human remains have become a home for sea creatures.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Deep Has Made of Us

We are the ones who went down with the galleys,
our bronze prows kissing the seafloor
like tired mouths finding rest at last.
We do not mourn ourselves anymore.

We have watched the years dissolve our names—
the ones etched in wax tablets, salt-eaten,
the ones our mothers called across courtyards
now syllables the current cannot hold.

Where our ribs once cradled breath,
small silver fish now school in shifting light,
darting through the hollow architecture
of what we used to be, unbothered by our stillness.

We have become reef and reliquary both.
The coins that filled our captains' chests
lie scattered now like strange, flat stones—
crabs have made their crossings over Caesar's face,

and octopi curl sleeping in our helmets,
dreaming boneless dreams in bronze,
ink-dark and patient, guarding nothing,
needing nothing that we understood as wealth.

Anemones have bloomed where wounds once opened,
soft and many-colored, waving slow
in currents that forget the storm that made them—
we are the garden grown from what we lost.

Sometimes the sunlight reaches down in shafts
and finds the gold still gleaming, dull and generous,
finds the white curve of what were once our hands
open now to barnacle and time.

We do not ask for mourning, do not need
the tears of those who walk the upper world.
We have become the deep's own furniture—
the coral now grows crowns where crowns were lost.

This is not tragedy anymore, but architecture:
the way the sea took hunger, took ambition,
took the desperate reaching of our voyage,
and built from it a home for smaller lives.

We are the reef. We are the treasury.
We are the quiet country fish call country.
What we were is compost for what swims here now—
and this, too, is a kind of going on.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine you are the collective voice of drowned soldiers from a first-century BC war fleet; write a reflective poem about your fate and the looted art that sank with you.
counterfactuals.output:
# Voices from the Deep

We went down with the bronze gods clutched in cargo holds,
Nereids and emperors, tangled in the same dark net—
looted from temples we never prayed in,
bound for shores we never reached.

The sea did not care whose blood was Roman,
whose was pirate, whose was slave.
It took us all the same,
opened its mouth and closed it
around ships and spoils and men
as if we were all equally its due.

We remember the weight of oars,
the salt-cracked hands, the orders shouted
over wind that would not listen.
We remember the marble faces
staring blank-eyed from their crates,
gods we were paid to steal
and paid, in the end, with our lives to carry.

Strange, how the statues survived us.
Their stone lips never needed air.
Their sculpted eyes did not fill with brine.
We became sediment, then silhouette, then story—
while Aphrodite kept her smile
through centuries of dark,
patient as only the already-dead can be.

Some diver's hand will find us, someday—
not us, but our shipwreck's signature:
a corroded sword hilt, a coin,
the bronze curve of a god's shoulder
we died still holding onto,
as if property could save us,
as if the empire's treasure
might float, and we might float with it.

It did not. We did not.

We are the nameless crew notes
in histories about the art we sank beside.
Scholars will date the bronze by its casting style,
argue provenance, debate which conquest
this particular god was stolen from—
and we will be the footnote:
*remains of the ship's company, unidentified.*

Let this be our epitaph, then, spoken in chorus
by drowned throats that still, somehow, remember how to speak:

We were men before we were cargo.
We had names before the sea erased them.
We carried beauty we did not make
into a grave none of us chose—
and the irony is not lost on us,
even now, even here,
that what we stole from history
is what history chose to save,

while we became the water itself,
the anonymous depth
that beauty rests in,
forever unremarked,
forever underneath.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
